description: Plain-English glossary for technical terms used in the UI (tooltips, §6.11). Max 25 words each.

records.definition: The internet's phone book: it turns website names into the numbers computers use to find each other.
A number that identifies one device or server on the internet, like a postal address.
A number identifying one organisation that routes internet traffic — an internet provider, company, or hosting provider.
Extra signatures that prove DNS answers really come from the right place and were not tampered with.
How long (in seconds) a DNS answer may be reused before asking again.
The modern replacement for WHOIS: who registered a domain name, and when it expires.
The old lookup service for domain ownership. Largely replaced by RDAP.
The DNS entry that says which servers accept this domain's email.
A DNS rule listing which servers may send email for a domain — it helps stop forged sender addresses.
A DNS rule telling receiving mail servers what to do when an email fails checks — plus reporting.
A digital signature added to outgoing email so receivers can verify it was not altered.
The digital document behind the padlock: it proves a site is who it claims and enables encryption.
Air Quality Index — one number summarising how clean or polluted the air is right now.
Tiny particles in the air small enough to enter the lungs — the main health risk from air pollution.
A 0–9 measure of geomagnetic activity: higher values mean aurora visible farther from the poles.
An earthquake's size on the logarithmic moment-magnitude scale — one whole number is about 32× more energy.
The world's reference time zone, formerly called GMT.
Short codes for airports and organisations (IATA: three letters like CDG; ICAO: four like LFPG).
A compact way to write a block of IP addresses, like 203.0.113.0/24 — the /24 says how many addresses.
The lookup that goes the other way: from an IP address back to a host name.
The three-digit result of a web request: 200 OK, 404 not found, 500 server error, and so on.
A security header telling browsers to always use the encrypted connection to this site.
A browser rule deciding which websites may fetch data from another website's servers.
A fibre-optic cable on the sea floor carrying internet traffic between continents.
A network of servers worldwide that copies website content closer to visitors so it loads faster.
